source_title: Effect of Residents' Previous Laparoscopic Surgery Experience on Initial Robotic Suturing Experience
summary_title: Effect of Residents' Previous Laparoscopic Surgery Experience on Initial Robotic Suturing Experience
executive_summary: This study investigated the impact of gynecology residents' prior laparoscopic experience on their robotic suturing skills and the value of structured dry-lab training. Thirteen gynecology residents with no prior robotic surgery experience were divided into two groups based on their laparoscopic experience: Group 1 (≤2 laparoscopic experiences) and Group 2 (≥3 laparoscopic experiences). Group 1 received dry-lab training before operating room experience. The primary finding was that residents with more laparoscopic experience (Group 2) showed a non-significant trend towards faster robotic suturing times compared to Group 1. Residents in Group 1 had a significantly lower mean suture time than residents in Group 2 for laparoscopic suturing (P = 0.009). For all residents, the average time for laparoscopic suturing was 382 ± 159 seconds, while robotic suturing took 326 ± 196 seconds (P = 0.12). The study suggests that prior laparoscopic experience might benefit robotic surgery learning, although the difference was not statistically significant. The study also supports the importance of dry-lab training. The main limitation is the small sample size, which may have affected the statistical power.
methodological_details: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of Texas Medical Branch. Thirteen gynecology residents participated: four PGY3s and nine PGY4s. None had prior robotic surgery experience. All residents received a didactic lecture on MIS suturing. Group 1 included all PGY3s and two MIS-naive PGY4s. Group 2 comprised the more MIS-experienced PGY4s (≥3 previous MIS experiences). Residents were evaluated using robotic suturing with intracorporeal knot tying and laparoscopic suturing using extracorporeal knot tying. The vaginal cuff was closed using a 0 polyglactin (Vicryl, Ethicon) on a CT-1 needle in an interrupted suture closure. Suture time was the elapsed time for loading the needle, placing four square knots, and cutting the suture. Statistical analysis used a t-test to compare mean suturing times by surgery modality and resident group. The Satterthwaite correction was applied when heterogeneity of variances was significant. The study design was a comparative, observational study. No information on randomization, blinding, or preregistration was provided. The study did not mention any specific multiple-comparison corrections. No demographic information beyond PGY level was provided.
procedures_architectures: The study involved two surgical techniques: robotic suturing using the da Vinci Surgical System (Intuitive Surgical, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) and laparoscopic suturing. The robotic system provides surgeons with greater dexterity and improved visualization. The laparoscopic suturing used extracorporeal knot tying. The study did not provide details on the specific da Vinci system model or the laparoscopic equipment used. All residents received a didactic lecture on MIS suturing. Group 1 (PGY3s and two PGY4s) received dry-lab training in suturing before operating room experience. The PGY4s with more experience did not receive additional dry-lab training. The procedure involved closing the vaginal cuff with interrupted sutures using a 0 polyglactin suture on a CT-1 needle. The primary outcome was the time taken to complete the suturing task, including loading the needle, placing four square knots, and cutting the suture. The study did not specify the exact dry-lab training protocol or the type of simulation used.
key_results: The mean suturing times were compared between PGY3 and PGY4 residents. For all residents, the average time for laparoscopic suturing was 382 ± 159 seconds, and for robotic suturing, it was 326 ± 196 seconds (P = 0.12). PGY3s had a shorter suturing time than PGY4s in both robotic and laparoscopic suturing. The PGY4 group showed a statistically significant difference (P = 0.02) between robotic (337 ± 235 seconds) and laparoscopic suturing (457 ± 158 seconds). Comparing the combined robotic and laparoscopic suturing times, the difference between the PGY3 (310 ± 95.8 seconds) and PGY4 (393 ± 210.6 seconds) groups was statistically significant (P = 0.01). Residents in Group 1 had a significantly lower mean suture time than Group 2 for laparoscopic suturing (P = 0.009). The residents in Group 2 had a lower mean suture time on the robot compared to Group 1; however, this difference did not achieve significance (P = 0.5).
